title: Former Monroe Elementary student honored 72 years after Brown v. Board of Education - WIBW
content: TOPEKA, Kan. (WIBW) - Seventy-two years after the landmark decision to end racial segregation in public schools, Brown v. Board of Education’s legacy lives on in the Capital City. The Topeka High drumline opened Saturday’s commemoration with a performance at Monroe School, a historic site in Topeka and the entire United States. “Being a young African-American male, it’s really good to be able to step into such a high and rewarding position and it really gets to show everyone that you can really do whatever you put your mind to,” said Carter Ramirez-Jennings, a Topeka High drumline member. “Brown v. Board is so significant to Kansas, and without it, we would have no integrated schools. And myself, I am a person of color, so I would not be able to go that I am in today,” said Abigail Culbertson, another Topeka High drumline member. Rowena Johnson Sanders, now 89, grew up attending Monroe Elementary. She’s now being honored for her historic walk to get an education during a time when schools were segregated. “What kids go through now is a vast difference. Lives, they have changed quite a bit and it’s for the best,” Sanders said. In honor of her role as a former student at Monroe, the Topeka NAACP recognized the efforts she made in the pursuit of education without barriers. “Little old me? With a t-shirt? With my name on it? Are you kidding? But I was very proud that somebody thought that much to do this. I really didn’t think it was that important, but apparently it is, okay!” Sanders said.
